status: RESEARCH OUTPUT — PART 1 of 2 (CHILLI / COTTON / MAIZE). Companion to crops.diseases.part-ccm.json. Not merged into shared/i18n yet.
purpose: Farmer-facing strings for every i18n key referenced by crops.diseases.part-ccm.json. The knowledge file stores keys only (CropRegistry.js diseaseSchema: 'i18n key arrays — the API never returns display prose'); the prose lives here.

rules.englishIsSourced: Every English string is a plainly-worded rendering of text quoted in the matching entry's `publishedSymptoms` or `sourceRefs[].note` in crops.diseases.part-ccm.json. Nothing here says anything the sourced material does not.
rules.hindiIsNull: EVERY Hindi value is null. No Hindi-language official source was fetched in this pass, and CLAUDE.md rule 8 forbids unsourced agronomic translation. Machine translation of these strings is not acceptable — a Hindi-literate agronomist must author them. See gap G-HI-1.
rules.noDosage: docs/ai/ai-safety.md rule 3. No string contains a dose, a concentration, a pesticide or fertilizer product name, or a brand. Where the source recommends chemical control, the string routes the farmer to KVK / Kisan Call Centre 1800-180-1551 instead.
rules.noUnitConversion: Lesion sizes appear in the unit the source printed (inches for the two maize entries).
rules.phoneNumber: 1800-180-1551 is the Kisan Call Centre number named in docs/ai/ai-safety.md rule 3. It is the only number that appears.

keyCount.verifiedBy: node cross-check on 2026-08-13: every key referenced by crops.diseases.part-ccm.json exists in both `en` and `hi`, there are no orphan keys in either direction, and no `hi` value is non-null.

en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.symptom.1: Tender twigs die back from the tip downwards; the branches and stem then dry and wither.
en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.symptom.2: Flowers drop heavily. The flower stalk shrivels and dries, and the drying spreads from the flower stalk into the stem.
en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.symptom.3: Ripe fruits show small round spots at first, which spread into oblong black-green patches with a clear black or straw-coloured edge.
en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.symptom.4: Badly affected fruits turn straw-coloured, shrivel and dry up, and are less pungent. Affected plants carry few fruits and of low quality.
en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.inspect.1: Look at the tips of tender twigs for drying that runs from the tip downwards.
en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.inspect.2: Check ripe fruits for small round spots and for dark patches with a sharp black or straw-coloured edge.
en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.inspect.3: Watch the crop closely once flowering starts — infection usually begins when the crop is in flower.
en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.inspect.4: The disease shows up after the rains stop, when dew stays on the plants for long periods. Inspect on those days.
en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.nextStep.1: Collect and remove affected fruits and dried twigs from the field.
en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.nextStep.2: Use only disease-free seed next season — this disease is carried on seed.
en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.nextStep.3: Chemical sprays are published for this disease, but this app does not give doses. Contact your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551, before spraying anything.
en.disease.CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE.prevention.2: Remove affected fruits and dried twigs from the field instead of leaving them lying.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.symptom.1: Leaves show small round or irregular dark brown to black greasy spots.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.symptom.2: As the spots grow, the centre becomes lighter with a dark band of tissue around it, and the spots join into irregular patches.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.symptom.3: Badly affected leaves turn yellow and fall off.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.symptom.4: Leaf stalks and stems are also affected; stem infection makes canker-like rough growths and the branches wilt.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.symptom.5: Fruits show round, raised, water-soaked spots with a pale yellow border, which later turn brown and sink in the centre.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.inspect.1: Hold a leaf up to the light and look for small greasy dark spots whose centres have turned lighter with a dark ring around them.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.inspect.2: Check the stems and leaf stalks for canker-like rough growths and for wilting branches.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.inspect.3: Check fruits for raised water-soaked spots with a pale yellow edge.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.nextStep.1: Keep the field clean — remove affected plants and plant debris.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.nextStep.2: Take seed only from disease-free plants for the next crop.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.nextStep.3: Chemical sprays are published for this disease, but this app does not give doses. Contact your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT.prevention: Obtain seed only from disease-free plants.
Keep the field clean — field sanitation matters for this disease.
en.disease.CHILLI_CERCOSPORA_LEAF_SPOT.symp: Leaf spots are brown and round, with small to large light grey centres and dark brown edges.
Spots may grow to 1 cm or more across, and sometimes join together.
Stem, leaf-stalk and pod lesions also have light grey centres with dark borders, but they are usually oval rather than round.
Badly infected leaves fall off early, which reduces yield.
en.disease.CHILLI_CERCOSPORA_LEAF_SPOT.insp: Look for round brown spots with a pale grey centre, and check whether they have reached about 1 cm across.
Check stems, leaf stalks and pods for oval lesions with grey centres.
Inspect after humid, drizzly or windy weather, which helps this disease develop and spread.
en.disease.CHILLI_CERCOSPORA_LEAF_SPOT.next: Remove and destroy infected crop debris — the fungus survives in it.
Chemical sprays are published for this disease, but this app does not give doses. Contact your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.CHILLI_CERCOSPORA_LEAF_SPOT.prev: Remove and destroy infected crop debris after harvest, because the fungus survives in it.
en.disease.CHILLI_HEALTHY.inspect.1: No disease signs were found in this check. Keep looking at the crop regularly.
en.disease.CHILLI_HEALTHY.inspect.2: Turn leaves over and look at the underside — powdery mildew and bacterial leaf spot both show there first.
en.disease.CHILLI_HEALTHY.inspect.3: Look more closely once flowering begins, and again after the rains stop when dew stays on the plants.
en.disease.CHILLI_HEALTHY.prevention.2: Keep the field clean and remove crop debris.
en.disease.CHILLI_HEALTHY.prevention.3: Raise the nursery under a net house or a cover, to protect seedlings from insects that carry viruses.
en.disease.CHILLI_HEALTHY.prevention.4: Place yellow sticky traps in the field to watch for whitefly.
en.disease.CHILLI_HEALTHY.prevention.6: Raise two rows of maize or sorghum as a barrier crop for every five rows of chilli.
en.disease.CHILLI_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.symptom.1: Leaves curl towards the midrib and become deformed; the leaf margins curl upward, giving a cup-like appearance.
en.disease.CHILLI_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.symptom.2: Leaves are much smaller than normal and show yellowing between the veins.
en.disease.CHILLI_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.symptom.3: The plant is stunted, because the internodes are shortened.
en.disease.CHILLI_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.symptom.4: Flower buds drop before reaching full size, and the anthers carry no pollen.
en.disease.CHILLI_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.inspect.1: Compare new leaves with older ones lower down — affected leaves are much smaller.
en.disease.CHILLI_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.inspect.2: Look for upward cupping of the leaf margins and for yellowing between the veins.
en.disease.CHILLI_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.inspect.3: Check the underside of leaves for whitefly, which carries this virus.
Uproot infected plants and burn or bury them, so the virus does not spread further.

There is no cure for most virus diseases — management is cultural and aimed at the insect that carries it. Contact your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551, for local guidance. This app does not give doses.
en.disease.CHILLI_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS.preventio: Cover nursery beds with nylon net or straw to protect the seedlings.
Place yellow sticky traps in the field to watch for whitefly.
Raise two to three rows of maize or sorghum as a border crop around the field.
Avoid growing chilli after chilli in the same field year after year.
en.disease.CHILLI_NUTRIENT_DEFICIENCY.sympt: Leaves are light green or yellow, the plant grows slowly and stays small.
When nitrogen is short, the older lower leaves turn yellow first and may later turn brown and die.
When potassium is short, the edges of the older leaves look burned or scorched.
Older leaves may also show yellowing between the veins, or a purple colour, especially on the underside.
en.disease.CHILLI_NUTRIENT_DEFICIENCY.inspe: Note which leaves are affected — the older lower leaves, or the newest leaves at the top. The pattern is different for different nutrients.
Note whether the whole leaf is pale, only the edges are burned, or only the area between the veins has yellowed.
A photograph cannot say which nutrient is short. The same look can come from more than one nutrient, and insect or disease damage can look like a deficiency.
en.disease.CHILLI_NUTRIENT_DEFICIENCY.nextS: Get a soil test, and a plant test if you can. What you see on the leaf should only be used alongside soil and plant analysis, not instead of it.
Take an affected plant or a clear photo to your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551. This app does not give fertilizer doses.
en.disease.CHILLI_NUTRIENT_DEFICIENCY.preve: Test the soil before the season and plan nutrient application from the test result, rather than waiting for symptoms — by the time symptoms appear, yield has usually already been lost.
en.disease.CHILLI_POWDERY_MILDEW.symptom.1: A white powdery growth appears on the lower side of the leaves.
en.disease.CHILLI_POWDERY_MILDEW.symptom.2: Affected leaves are shed, which sharply reduces fruit yield.
en.disease.CHILLI_POWDERY_MILDEW.inspect.1: Turn the leaves over — the powdery growth is on the underside, not on the top.
en.disease.CHILLI_POWDERY_MILDEW.inspect.2: Check whether leaves are dropping from the plant.
en.disease.CHILLI_POWDERY_MILDEW.nextStep.1: Note the date you first saw the powdery growth. Published sprays are timed from the first appearance of the symptom.
en.disease.CHILLI_POWDERY_MILDEW.nextStep.2: Chemical sprays are published for this disease, but this app does not give doses. Contact your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
Small dark green water-soaked areas appear on the lower surface of the leaves; they become angular because the veins stop them spreading, and can then be seen on both leaf surfaces.
The angular spots later turn reddish brown, and the infection spreads into the veins and veinlets.
The veins and veinlets blacken, giving a blighted look, and bacterial ooze forms as crusts or scales on the lower leaf surface.
Leaves become crinkled and twisted inward, wither, and fall.
Dark brown to black lesions form on stems and fruiting branches; the stem cracks and the branch hangs as a dry black twig — the 'black arm' symptom.
Bolls show water-soaked lesions that turn into dark black sunken irregular spots; affected bolls shed or burst early, and the lint is stained yellow.
In seedlings, small water-soaked lesions appear on the cotyledons and the infection spreads through the leaf stalk to the stem, killing the seedling.
Look at the underside of leaves for dark green water-soaked patches with straight, angular edges set by the veins.
Check whether the veins themselves have turned black.
Check stems and fruiting branches for black lesions, cracking, and drooping black twigs.
Check bolls for sunken black spots and for early bursting.
This disease is favoured by high humidity (around 85 per cent) and by rain followed by bright sunshine. Inspect after such weather.
en.disease.COTTON_BACTERIAL_BLIGHT.nextStep: Remove and destroy infected plant debris.
Rogue out volunteer cotton plants and weed hosts.
Plan crop rotation with non-host crops for the next season.
Seed treatment and sprays are published for this disease, but this app does not give doses. Contact your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.COTTON_BACTERIAL_BLIGHT.preventi: Follow crop rotation with non-host crops.
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest — the bacterium survives in dried debris in the soil for several years.
Rogue out volunteer cotton plants and weed hosts.
en.disease.COTTON_CURL_VIRUS.symptom.2: The leaf veins thicken, and small leaf-like outgrowths (enations) appear on the underside of the leaves.
en.disease.COTTON_CURL_VIRUS.symptom.3: In severe infection all the leaves are curled, growth is held back, and the plant carries fewer bolls.
en.disease.COTTON_CURL_VIRUS.inspect.1: Turn leaves over and look for thickened veins and small leaf-like outgrowths on the underside. These are the signs that separate this from other causes of curling.
en.disease.COTTON_CURL_VIRUS.inspect.2: Check how many leaves on the plant are curled, and whether the plant's growth has slowed.
en.disease.COTTON_CURL_VIRUS.inspect.3: Look for whitefly, which carries this virus.
en.disease.COTTON_CURL_VIRUS.nextStep.1: Remove volunteer perennial cotton plants and other host plants nearby, including wild okra and related plants, which keep the virus alive through the year.
en.disease.COTTON_CURL_VIRUS.nextStep.2: The virus is carried by whitefly. It is not spread by seed and not spread by touch, so handling plants does not pass it on.
en.disease.COTTON_CURL_VIRUS.nextStep.3: Contact your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551, for local guidance. This app does not give doses.
en.disease.COTTON_CURL_VIRUS.prevention.1: Adjust the planting date to avoid the peak whitefly period.
en.disease.COTTON_CURL_VIRUS.prevention.2: Remove volunteer perennial cotton and other host plants around the field.
en.disease.COTTON_HEALTHY.inspect.1: No disease signs were found in this check. Keep looking at the crop regularly.
en.disease.COTTON_HEALTHY.inspect.2: Turn leaves over — bacterial blight patches and leafhopper nymphs both show on the underside first.
en.disease.COTTON_HEALTHY.inspect.3: Inspect after rain followed by bright sunshine, which favours bacterial blight.
en.disease.COTTON_HEALTHY.prevention.1: Follow crop rotation with non-host crops.
en.disease.COTTON_HEALTHY.prevention.2: Remove and destroy infected plant debris.
en.disease.COTTON_HEALTHY.prevention.3: Rogue out volunteer cotton plants and weed hosts.
en.disease.COTTON_HEALTHY.prevention.4: Adjust the planting date to avoid the peak whitefly period.
Stems and leaf stalks twist and curl.
Leaves are out of proportion — unusually long and narrow, which is called strapping — and the leaf veins look abnormal.
With some herbicides the plant yellows all over, starting on the newest leaves and spreading to the whole plant.
Check whether the damage starts on the newest growth at the top of the plant.
Look at the shape of the new leaves — long and narrow, twisted, or with odd-looking veins, rather than spotted.

This is chemical injury, not an infection. It cannot be told apart from a nutrient problem or a disease from a photograph alone, and the published guidance says even different herbicides are difficult or impossible to tell apart from the symptoms.
en.disease.COTTON_HERBICIDE_DAMAGE.nextStep: This is reported as an observation, not a diagnosis. This app gives no treatment for herbicide injury.
Take an affected plant or a clear photo to your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.COTTON_LEAF_HOPPER_JASSIDS.sympt: Leaves curl downward and turn red.
Under heavy attack the leaves turn brick red.
Plant growth is held back, and plants may die.
en.disease.COTTON_LEAF_HOPPER_JASSIDS.inspe: Turn leaves over and look between the veins on the underside for light green, see-through, wingless nymphs. Finding the insect is what tells this apart from leaf reddening caused by other things.
Look for small green wedge-shaped adult hoppers on the crop.
Count them. The published action level is 50 nymphs or adults across 50 leaves.
en.disease.COTTON_LEAF_HOPPER_JASSIDS.nextS: Keep the field free of weeds.
Apply nitrogen fertilizer judiciously — do not over-apply.
If counts reach the published action level of 50 hoppers across 50 leaves, contact your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551, before spraying. This app does not give doses.
en.disease.COTTON_LEAF_HOPPER_JASSIDS.preve: Grow hairy (hirsute) cotton varieties, which are less affected.
Adopt synchronised sowing with the fields around you.
Keep the field free of weeds and apply nitrogen fertilizer judiciously.
en.disease.COTTON_LEAF_REDDENING.symptom.1: The leaves turn red. This is a disorder, not an infection, and the redness is caused by red pigment building up in the leaf.
en.disease.COTTON_LEAF_REDDENING.inspect.1: First turn the leaves over and look for leafhoppers on the underside. Leafhopper attack also reddens cotton leaves, and finding the insect changes what the problem is.
en.disease.COTTON_LEAF_REDDENING.inspect.2: Reddening has many published causes — magnesium shortage, low nitrogen in the leaf or soil, a sudden fall in night temperature, hot days with cold nights, water stress, and waterlogging. A photograph cannot tell which one it is, and more than one may be acting together.
en.disease.COTTON_LEAF_REDDENING.nextStep.1: This is reported as an observation, not a diagnosis. This app gives no fertilizer or spray recommendation for leaf reddening.
en.disease.COTTON_LEAF_REDDENING.nextStep.2: Take an affected plant or a clear photo to your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551. A soil test will help, since some of the published causes are soil-related.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.symptom.1: Tiny flecks appear on both sides of the leaves.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.symptom.2: These become round to elongated cinnamon-brown powdery pustules that break through both leaf surfaces.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.symptom.3: As the crop matures, the pustules turn brownish black.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.symptom.4: In severe cases the infection spreads to the leaf sheath and other parts.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.inspect.1: Rub a pustule with your finger — rust pustules leave a brown powder on the skin.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.inspect.2: Check both the upper and lower surfaces of the leaf; the pustules break through on both sides.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.inspect.3: This disease is favoured by cool, moist weather, around 15 to 25 degrees Celsius.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.nextStep.1: Remove the alternate host weeds (Oxalis species) from around the field — the disease carries over on them.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.nextStep.2: Collect the crop remains and destroy them by burning or burying.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.nextStep.3: Foliar sprays are published for this disease, but this app does not give doses. Contact your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.prevention.1: Remove alternate host weeds (Oxalis species) from around the field.
en.disease.MAIZE_COMMON_RUST.prevention.2: Collect and destroy crop remains after harvest by burning or burying.
en.disease.MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT.symptom.1: Long, narrow, rectangular lesions, up to about 2 inches long, that start light tan and later turn grey.
en.disease.MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT.symptom.2: The lesions are bounded by the leaf veins, so their edges are straight and they run along the leaf.
en.disease.MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT.symptom.3: Lesions may join together and kill whole leaves.
en.disease.MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT.symptom.4: Symptoms appear on the lower leaves first, about two to three weeks before tasselling.
en.disease.MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT.inspect.1: Start with the lower leaves — this problem shows there first.
en.disease.MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT.inspect.2: Look at the edges of the lesion. If they are straight and stop dead at the veins, that points to grey leaf spot rather than leaf blight, whose lesions are cigar-shaped and taper at the ends.
en.disease.MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT.inspect.3: Look for it around two to three weeks before tasselling, after warm and very humid weather.
en.disease.MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT.nextStep.1: Plan crop rotation and tillage for the next season — both reduce how much of the fungus survives in the residue.
en.disease.MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT.nextStep.2: Ask about resistant hybrids for your area at your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
Use resistant hybrids where they are available for your area.
Follow crop rotation and tillage, which reduce survival of the fungus in crop residue.
en.disease.MAIZE_HEALTHY.inspect.1: No disease signs were found in this check. Keep looking at the crop regularly.
en.disease.MAIZE_HEALTHY.inspect.2: Start with the lower leaves — leaf blight and grey leaf spot both show there first.
en.disease.MAIZE_HEALTHY.inspect.3: Check both surfaces of the leaf; rust pustules break through on both sides.
en.disease.MAIZE_HEALTHY.inspect.4: Check again around two to three weeks before tasselling.
en.disease.MAIZE_HEALTHY.prevention.1: Burn or bury infected maize stubble after harvest.
en.disease.MAIZE_HEALTHY.prevention.2: Collect crop remains and destroy them by burning or burying.
en.disease.MAIZE_HEALTHY.prevention.3: Remove alternate host weeds (Oxalis species) from around the field.
en.disease.MAIZE_NORTHERN_LEAF_BLIGHT.sympt: Long cigar-shaped lesions, grey-green to tan, appear on the lower leaves.
The tan lesions are slender and oblong and taper at the ends, ranging from 1 to 6 inches long.
Lesions run parallel to the leaf margins, join together, and can cover the whole leaf.
Spores form on the underside of the leaf, and below the lesions the fungus gives a dusty black-green fuzzy appearance.
Leaves become greyish-green and brittle, resembling leaves killed by frost.
en.disease.MAIZE_NORTHERN_LEAF_BLIGHT.inspe: Look at the lesion shape. Cigar-shaped lesions that taper at both ends point to leaf blight, while rectangular lesions that stop dead at the veins point to grey leaf spot.
Turn the leaf over and look under a lesion for a dusty black-green fuzz.
This disease is favoured by wet, humid, cool weather later in the growing season.
en.disease.MAIZE_NORTHERN_LEAF_BLIGHT.nextS: Burn or bury infected maize stubble — the fungus survives on infected plant debris.
Foliar sprays are published for this disease, but this app does not give doses. Contact your nearest KVK, or call the Kisan Call Centre on 1800-180-1551.
en.disease.MAIZE_NORTHERN_LEAF_BLIGHT.preve: Burn or bury infected maize stubble after harvest.
